events.excerpt: Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors. Two weeks and a slow prototype Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school. That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow. events.excerpt: In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind , I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system. Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany: Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change. In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm. We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. events.excerpt: Between 24 and 26 October 2026, a bug in the XCM executor on Polkadot Asset Hub was used to reduce the recorded issuance of dotUSD without changing underlying account balances. The recorded issuance is expected to equal the sum of all account balances. By reducing the recorded issuance without changing any account’s balance, the attacker broke this assumption within the protocol. This discrepancy affected pricing in the Hub’s DOT/dotUSD pool on the decentralised exchange and enabled trades at an artificial exchange rate. The estimated loss was approximately $1.381 million in DOT value. At the time of the attack, the Polkadot Treasury was the only liquidity provider in the pool. No users lost any funds. The available on-chain evidence has not established that the attacker who exploited the XCM vulnerability also profited from the subsequent arbitrage. Furthermore, the bug did not remove dotUSD from account balances, but the understated recorded issuance restricted redemption capacity pending a correction. What happened XCM programs are meant to be transactional. That is, when a program fails, none of the state changes from that program are applied. There was a bug present that did not follow this behavior in certain circumstances. The issue was first reported to Parity through its
events.headline: XCM Incident Review: What happened and what we learned

events.excerpt: A growing class of protocols needs to persist one tiny fact per event, forever: this nullifier is spent, this nonce is used, this session share is settled. Privacy pools write a nullifier per withdrawal. Unordered nonce schemes (Permit2’s nonceBitmap , EIP-4337-style two-dimensional nonces) write replay flags because they cannot guarantee sequenced nonces. Machine-scale settlement (DePIN connectivity, bandwidth, compute) writes a mark per settled session. Call all of it what it is: replay protection, and its cost is pure storage. ZK batching has made the compute side nearly free: one proof verifies thousands of signatures or membership checks at flat cost. The flags are what no longer compress. The progression every protocol rediscovers. Worst case, and still the most common shape: mapping(bytes32 => bool) used; // one flag, one slot // every flag: ~22,100 gas (20,000 zero-to-nonzero + 2,100 cold access), state forever This is what nullifier sets look like: the key is a hash, so no two flags ever share a slot, and nothing amortizes. First optimization, 256 flags per word, when flag ids are dense: mapping(uint256 => uint256) bitmap; // key = flagId >> 8, bit = flagId & 255 // first flag in a word: ~22,100; each later flag: ~5,000 (2,100 access + 2,900 reset, own tx) This is Permit
events.headline: Storage-optimized replay protection: from hash => bool to packed flag lanes, and can the protocol offer better?

events.excerpt: TL;DR: XCMv3 will be removed in polkadot-sdk stable2612 (release 2026-12-17, ingestion by fellowship runtimes only after that). Once system chains upgrade, they will no longer send or accept v3 messages. If your chain or your app still uses v3, you need to move to v4 or v5 before then. Check your chain on the dashboard: XCM Versions . XCMv5 was merged in November 2024: XCM v5 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #4826 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub . A PR removing v3 ( Remove XCMv3 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #13629 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub ) will ship in stable2612 , scheduled for 2026-12-17 . After that, system parachains and any other runtime can adopt it. Allowing for runtime releases and governance, expect the first chains to drop v3 in early 2027. Once a chain drops v3, it can’t decode v3 messages sent to it and can’t downgrade outgoing messages to v3. XCM between that chain and any other chain still on v3 will fail. To help, I built a dashboard ( XCM Versions ) showing each chains’ XCM version. Click a chain to see suggested action items. The main ones are: Code: move XCM programs and types to v4+. This is mostly renames (e.g. dropping the Multi prefix). Raw v3 types in storage don’t need migrating because the encoding is the same, but stored Versioned*

events.excerpt: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022 , the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions. Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver . In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings. Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed? It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many C

events.excerpt: tl;dr Open-bidding with random deadline (candle auctions) and few auction participants can lead to higher bidder profits than sealed-bid auctions. This is already true in a one-shot auction without explicit coordination or collusion. For the Ethereum builder-market post-Glamsterdam, I conjecture that this gives current participants a strong incentive to maintain the current open-bid auction by restricting outside bidding and per-missioning participation in relay auctions. In this post I want to formalize a piece of folk knowledge which I think is well-known among many searchers, builders and other participants of the MEV ecosystem: Open bidding auctions with a random deadline and few participants tend to give those participants more payoff than a sealed auction. On a high level, the logic is straightforward. Uncertainty about the auction deadline (in the case of PoS Ethereum through heterogeneous proposer behavior (timing games) and locations) creates for equally fast bidders with equal value a quasi-lottery: Bidders can outbid each other in small increments and whoever manages to place the last bid before the auction ends wins. This is preferable for them to bidding their full value away in a sealed auction (with certain deadline). The idea dates back to Ethereum PoW times where
events.headline: Why searchers and builders like candle auctions (and why it matters for the builder market post-Glamsterdam)

events.excerpt: Summary Rollups scaled by moving execution off the L1, but the authentication part of every transaction still goes to the L1. That makes data the likely bottleneck for L2 scaling in the PQ era, even with more blobs. PQ signatures are far larger than ECDSA, so if every L2 user switched to one, signatures would make up 99% of transaction data and the transfers that fit in 6 blobs would fall from about 6,600 to 155. ZK applications have it worse, since a single PQ proof usually does not fit in 3 blobs. Either way, the bottleneck is that the cost of checking trust grows with the number of users. An L2 can cut this cost by adopting EIP-8288: signatures and proofs move out of transactions, and the statements of many blocks are bundled into one leanVM aggregate proof posted to the L1. A transaction authenticated with leanSPHINCS then compresses to 100 to 129 bytes, close to an ECDSA transaction. A 32-core machine (AWS c7a.8xlarge) can prove up to 170 leanSPHINCS signatures per second on a 2-second chain. At that load, the 2,040 leanSPHINCS transactions arriving per L1 block fit in 2.8 to 3.3 blobs on average, calculated from the measured aggregate size and compression ratio. Without EIP-8288 aggregates, carrying the signatures in the transactions would take 79 blobs for the same transac
events.headline: It's time to scale the trust: EIP-8288 on OP Stack

events.excerpt: Most key-compromise defenses today (smart wallets, ERC-7579 modules, social recovery, EIP-7702 delegation) enforce policy in the account’s code. ERC-8403 continues this: spend limits and unlock times are authorities committed under the account’s root. I’d like to probe a different placement: enforcing rate limits at the asset : the token contract for ERC-20s, and eventually the protocol itself for native ETH. Motivation. Account-level policy only binds while the account’s code is in the transfer path. Two gaps: Allowances : a contract holding an existing transferFrom approval moves tokens without re-entering the wallet’s validation logic, so a wallet-level daily limit does not bind. Delegation replacement : under EIP-7702, the compromised EOA key can re-delegate and strip the policy that was supposed to contain it. An asset-level check binds every balance-reducing path ( transfer , transferFrom , burns) regardless of which application initiated it, and survives delegation changes. Sketch (details negotiable, that is the point of the thread): Optional per-account spending limit (rolling window) enforced where balances change. Security-weakening changes (raising or removing a limit, replacing a recovery address) take effect after a delay of about 14 days; security-strengthening cha
events.headline: Asset-level spending limits and recovery: should rate limiting live in the asset rather than the account?

events.excerpt: Abstract PropAMMs are on-chain venues whose prices are set by a single maker. The maker pushes quote state on-chain, and fills read that state. We decoded 92,627 fills on nine Ethereum PropAMMs over 30 days (10 September to 9 October 2026) from execution data. We priced the 69,827 WETH/stablecoin fills against Binance one-second trades. Three of the registry venues accept maker state only if it is stamped with the current block’s timestamp. Their fills always execute against an update in the same block. Takers pay about 0.45 bp at the fill, on every one of the 30 days. Over the following five minutes the price does not move in their favour on average, in any taker class: there is no sign of adverse selection. Of fills after a CEX move of more than 0.5 bp in the preceding 12 seconds, 78.5% trade against it. The PropAMM quote follows the CEX in the same block, while Uniswap lags. Arbitrage contracts and routers use the PropAMM as the fresh side of a trade against a stale AMM. Fills are priced no later than their block’s sealing, which relays received 0.1 to 3.1 s after the slot start on the two days measured. Markouts change by under 0.1 bp across that range. events.excerpt: ⚠️ Security: CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel) CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. It is not specific to MPTCP, but the demonstrated remote exploit requires an MPTCP listener, which Go 1.24+ enables by default. This release disables MPTCP listeners in lnd by default , which closes the demonstrated exploit path through lnd. It is a mitigation, not a fix: the kernel patch is the only fix. Linux operators should: Upgrade to this release. Disable MPTCP on the host ( sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 ), since other services on the machine are not covered by this release. Install a patched kernel as soon as your distribution ships one. If you cannot upgrade yet, start your existing binary with the environment variable GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 , which turns off Go's default MPTCP listeners. Do not set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=1 to re-enable MPTCP until your kernel is patched. The Go team's discussion of the issue is at golang/go#82717 . See the release notes for the full instructions, including Docker and firewall guidance. Windows and macOS are not affected. Database Migrations There are no migrations in this release.
